paragraph: Specifying the scope of use of a dataset is an important step before sharing it [ 41]. Particularly, it is known that data-driven models are not reliable and may be unfair towards the groups that are not well represented in their (training) dataset [ 36,37]. Therefore, it is im- portant to identify the potential groups that are under-represented ∗This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation, Grant No. 2348919 and 2107290. However, data in practice often misses to include demographic information of entities. Even in cases where some demographic information are available, many others may be missing that is necessary for identifying representa- tion bias [ 38]. To further motivate this problem, let us consider the following example: Example 1. A data-sharing platform (e.g., Chicago Open Data Portal [2]) would like to responsibly specify the under-represented andunder-performing groups in their shared data in order to limit their scope of use. However, their datasets either do not include grouping attributes (such as race) or only contain some of those. Moreover, targeting a comprehensive audit, they do not want to limit their scope to a small set of predefined groups. Instead, they want to be proactive in their detection process, even for the groups they might have missed to consider. For some cases such as image datasets, when a small and prede- termined set of grouping attributes (e.g., gender ) are missing, one may be able to use techniques such as crowdsourcing to identify under-represented groups based on those attributes [ 31]. Our prob- lem, however, is that the grouping attributes are not predetermined. In other words, we consider an unknown unknown situation where not only do we lack access to the grouping attributes but we also do not know the groups of interest. To address this problem, we introduce the problem of mining the potential groups that are under-represented and under-performing, when the grouping attributes are unknown. We refer to this prob- lem as Minoria mining . To the best of our knowledge, this paper isthe first to introduce and study the Minoria mining problem . In simple terms, the main question we want to answer in this paper is, “are there regions in data-space, representing potential groups that are (a) under-represented, for which (b) the model under-performs ?” For instance, aligned with Example 1, our experi- ments on a Crimes dataset (§ 7.1.1) identified North-side Chicago as under-represented and under-performing. This information helps the model developers and data owners such as Chicago Open Data Portal to proactively identify a potential issue, decide if it is socially concerning, and limit the dataset’s scope-of-use accordingly. Similar to any other data mining problem, multiple approaches may come to mind for addressing this problem. For example, one can adapt a clustering technique (such as k-means clustering [ 28] or subspace and projective clustering [ 24,29,32]) to cluster the data into potential groups. However, as we shall show in our experi- ments (§ 7.1.2) such an approach fails to identify under-represented groups, simply because there are not enough instances from those groups in the dataset. This is a well-known drawback of the clus- tering methods, that their performance degrades substantially for

In this section, we start by studying the problem in R2– referred to as the 2D case. Before providing the technical details, we would like to clarify that in the 2D case, Dcan have more than two observation attributes (used for prediction). However, the projection directions are considered with respect to a pair of observation attributes called attributes of interest. For example, in our experiments in § 7, we uselongitude and latitude as the attributes of interest for Minoria mining in a crime dataset. Recall that our goal is to find a set of high-skew directions. Let H={d(ti)|ti∈D} be the set of dual hyper-planes in the dual space and letEbe an oracle that returns An 2(the ordered list of vertices in then 2-th level of arrangement of H) inTenum time. GivenAn 2, we can iterate through the neighboring median re- gions by iterating through the elements (vertices) of this ordered list. Based on Theorem 2, within each median region, the high-skew direction is either at the boundary points (two vertices of the line 4Due to the space limitations, the proof is provided in the technical report [16]. segment) or at a specific direction, which can be calculated in O(d). Since this time is dominated by the time taken to calculate the skew value of the directions corresponding to the boundary points, we can ignore it while analyzing the complexity of our algorithm. In the second phase of our algorithm, we should iterate through the neighboring median regions and calculate the skew value of the directions of the boundaries of these regions. We want to return the top-lhigh-skew directions as the Minoria candidates. In order to do that, we use a Max-Heap data structure to push these directions based on their skew value. We define Tskew as the running time of this phase. In the end, we pop the top- ldirections from the heap, evaluate the model on the tail of these directions, and check the error on the tail to see if it represents an under-represented group candidate. A visualization of this approach is provided in Figure 3. LetTpopbe the time complexity of the final step. Then, the overall time complexity of the algorithm is T=Tenum+Tskew+Tpop. Having discussed the overall description of the 2D solution, let us next explain the oracle Efor enumeratingAn 2.
Our efficient algorithm (§ 4.3) takes An 2, then 2-th level in an or- dered list, as the input. The k-th level of arrangement in R2has a complexity (the number of its vertices) of m=O(n.k1 3)[17].

There are efficient deterministic and randomized algorithms for enumerating the k-th level. The SOTA deterministic algorithm is by Timothy Chan [ 10]. It enumeratesAkas an ordered list in O(nlogm+mlog1+αn), whereαis a small positive constant, nis the number of hyperplanes, and mis the number of vertices in the k-th level of arrangement. The generalized Ray-sweeping algorithm suffers from the curse of dimensionality [21]. Therefore, in this section, we propose practical solutions based on search-space discretization (§ 6.1) and smart exploration of the projection space (§ 6.2 and 6.3).

Without loss of generality, we adapt the epsilon-greedy ap- proach [ 42]. Defineε≤1as the exploration probability. We flip a coin with probability εin each iteration and choose to explore or exploit based on this trial result. Let f′be the best-known solution with the maximum skew so far while considering a hyper-parameter τ′for the cosine similarity of the exploitation phase. During each exploration step, we draw random directions in the space of all possible directions. On the other hand, during the exploitation, we select the best-known direction f′and select a random direc- tion from the space of possible direction in the τ-vicinity of f′, defined as{f(s)|cos(f′,f(s))≤τ′}. This problem can be reduced to the problem of sampling uniformly from the surface of a unit d-dimensional spherical cone with the center f′and the angular radius ofτ. We use the sampling approach proposed in [8].

Results. The top- 2high-skew directions are shown in Fig 4. As we can see, the first two high-skew directions are along the north side to the south side of Chicago. We select 0.01,0.001, and 0.0001 percentile of the points in the tail of the high-skew projected points. The tails of the high-skew directions are presented using the or- ange regions. Evidently, in both cases, the tails correspond to the North-side Chicago . To provide some background about the city, Chicago is one of the most segregated cities in the US, with the vast majority of its north side being White .8We refer the curious reader to [ 18,30] for more details. North-side is under-represented in the dataset for many reasons, such as predictive policing [15]. At the same time, the f1-score significantly decreases on the tail of the projection, illustrating that predictions based on the crime dataset are not accurate for this group. To provide more details about these directions, we provide the tail-performance for different percentiles for these two directions in Tables 1 and 2. The College-admission dataset [ 3] con- tains details about a group of students who sent applications to US universities. This dataset has 400 rows and 7 columns indicating the features of the submitted applications (like GRE, GPA, Gender/Race, etc.). The female-to-male ratio in this dataset is around 1.1.
